warmup.q: The bus from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus stores handlers in a map keyed by event::class. You subscribe an audit handler under PaymentEvent::class and publish a PaymentCaptured. How many times does the audit handler run?
options: Once: a PaymentCaptured is a PaymentEvent
Never: no event's run-time class is the interface PaymentEvent
It doesn't compile: you can't subscribe under an interface
Twice: once for the class and once for the interface
warmup.why: The lookup uses the event's exact run-time class, PaymentCaptured, and nobody subscribed under that key. The subscription itself compiles, because PaymentEvent::class is a KClass<PaymentEvent>. Delivering to supertypes takes a walk up the event's type hierarchy, which this lesson adds.

sections.h: Route by the event's class, then walk up its supertypes
sections.html:
Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus built a bus that keys handlers by event::class. It has a hole you met in the warm-up: an audit handler subscribed under PaymentEvent::class never runs, because no event's run-time class is the interface itself. The same goes for a handler of MoneyMovement. Lesson 1 of this track made that middle level on purpose, so the bus has to honor it.

There are two honest fixes. The first keeps one flat list of (type, handler) pairs and asks type.isInstance(event) of each. It is short and correct, and every publish checks every subscription: forty handlers, forty checks per event, almost all of them misses. The second keeps the registry keyed by KClass, as KClass, Class and type tokens did, and works out for each event class the list of keys to visit: the class itself, then each supertype that is an event, nearest first.

Java
static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) {
    LinkedHashSet<Class<?>> found = new LinkedHashSet<>();
    ArrayDeque<Class<?>> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(type));
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        Class<?> c = queue.removeFirst();
        if (!PaymentEvent.class.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue;
        queue.addAll(List.of(c.getInterfaces()));
        if (c.getSuperclass() != null) queue.add(c.getSuperclass());
    }
    return List.copyOf(found);
}
Kotlin
private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) {
    val found = LinkedHashSet<Class<*>>()
    val queue = ArrayDeque<Class<*>>().apply { add(type) }
    while (queue.isNotEmpty()) {
        val c = queue.removeFirst()
        if (!PaymentEvent::class.java.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue
        queue.addAll(c.interfaces)
        c.superclass?.let(queue::add)
    }
    found.map { it.kotlin }
}

For PaymentCaptured the walk gives [PaymentCaptured, MoneyMovement, PaymentEvent], and publish looks up only those three keys. The breadth-first order is a promise to callers: specific handlers run before general ones, and within one key, in subscription order. Guava's EventBus routes the same way, to subscribers of "any type to which the event is assignable", and caches the flattened hierarchy per class.

The walk uses Java reflection, getInterfaces() and getSuperclass(), which costs no extra jar. kotlin-reflect's allSuperclasses would also work, but that lesson's rule applies: describing a class needs the 3.8 MB kotlin-reflect at run time, and naming and casting don't. The answer never changes for a class, so computeIfAbsent caches it once per class. On a ConcurrentHashMap that call is one atomic step, so two threads publishing the first capture at once don't race to fill the cache.

code.title: DispatchDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.dispatch import workbench.events.l02.demo.MoneyMovement import workbench.events.l02.demo.PaymentCaptured import workbench.events.l02.demo.PaymentDeclined import workbench.events.l02.demo.PaymentEvent import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.cast // The event model (PaymentEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. /** Keys every handler by the class it was subscribed under; delivery can look up keys two ways. */ class Bus(private val walkSupertypes: Boolean) { private val handlers = HashMap<KClass<*>, MutableList<(PaymentEvent) -> Unit>>() fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: (E) -> Unit) { handlers.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() }.add { event -> handler(type.cast(event)) } } fun publish(event: PaymentEvent) { val keys = if (walkSupertypes) dispatchKeys(event.javaClass) else listOf(event::class) for (key in keys) handlers[key]?.forEach { it(event) } } } /** The event's class, then its supertypes that are events, nearest first. */ fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> { val found = LinkedHashSet<Class<*>>() val queue = ArrayDeque(listOf(type)) while (queue.isNotEmpty()) { val c = queue.removeFirst() if (!PaymentEvent::class.java.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue queue.addAll(c.interfaces) c.superclass?.let(queue::add) } return found.map { it.kotlin } } fun main() { for (walk in listOf(false, true)) { val ran = mutableListOf<String>() val bus = Bus(walk) bus.subscribe(PaymentEvent::class) { ran += "audit" } bus.subscribe(MoneyMovement::class) { ran += "movements" } bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured::class) { ran += "ledger" } bus.publish(PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)) println("%-22s %s".format(if (walk) "walking supertypes:" else "exact class only:", ran)) } println("keys for PaymentCaptured: " + dispatchKeys(PaymentCaptured::class.java).map { it.simpleName }) println("keys for PaymentDeclined: " + dispatchKeys(PaymentDeclined::class.java).map { it.simpleName }) }

alt.title: DispatchDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.dispatch; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.LinkedHashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class DispatchDemoJava { sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentAuthorized, PaymentDeclined, MoneyMovement { String paymentId(); } record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, long cents) implements PaymentEvent {} record PaymentDeclined(String paymentId, String reason) implements PaymentEvent {} sealed interface MoneyMovement extends PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured, PaymentRefunded { long cents(); } record PaymentCaptured(String paymentId, long cents) implements MoneyMovement {} record PaymentRefunded(String paymentId, long cents) implements MoneyMovement {} /** Keys every handler by the class it was subscribed under; delivery can look up keys two ways. */ static final class Bus { private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>>> handlers = new HashMap<>(); private final boolean walkSupertypes; Bus(boolean walkSupertypes) { this.walkSupertypes = walkSupertypes; } <E extends PaymentEvent> void subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) { handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(event -> handler.accept(type.cast(event))); } void publish(PaymentEvent event) { List<Class<?>> keys = walkSupertypes ? dispatchKeys(event.getClass()) : List.of(event.getClass()); for (Class<?> key : keys) handlers.getOrDefault(key, List.of()).forEach(h -> h.accept(event)); } } /** The event's class, then its supertypes that are events, nearest first. */ static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { LinkedHashSet<Class<?>> found = new LinkedHashSet<>(); ArrayDeque<Class<?>> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(type)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { Class<?> c = queue.removeFirst(); if (!PaymentEvent.class.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue; queue.addAll(List.of(c.getInterfaces())); if (c.getSuperclass() != null) queue.add(c.getSuperclass()); } return List.copyOf(found); } public static void main(String[] args) { for (boolean walk : new boolean[] {false, true}) { List<String> ran = new ArrayList<>(); Bus bus = new Bus(walk); bus.subscribe(PaymentEvent.class, e -> ran.add("audit")); bus.subscribe(MoneyMovement.class, e -> ran.add("movements")); bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured.class, e -> ran.add("ledger")); bus.publish(new PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)); System.out.printf("%-22s %s%n", walk ? "walking supertypes:" : "exact class only:", ran); } System.out.println("keys for PaymentCaptured: " + dispatchKeys(PaymentCaptured.class).stream().map(Class::getSimpleName).toList()); System.out.println("keys for PaymentDeclined: " + dispatchKeys(PaymentDeclined.class).stream().map(Class::getSimpleName).toList()); } }

try.expect: exact class only: [ledger] and walking supertypes: [ledger, movements, audit]. The keys are [PaymentCaptured, MoneyMovement, PaymentEvent] and [PaymentDeclined, PaymentEvent]. After your change the second list is [ledger, movements, audit again, audit]: keys go nearest first, and within the MoneyMovement key the handlers run in subscription order.

sections.h: Handlers only consume events, so declare them in
sections.html:
A handler only ever takes an event in. It never hands one back. That makes it a consumer, and Contravariance with in: consumers gave the rule: declare the type parameter in.

Java
@FunctionalInterface
interface Handler<E extends PaymentEvent> { void handle(E event); }    // Java: invariant

<E extends PaymentEvent> Subscription subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { ... }
Kotlin
fun interface Handler<in E : PaymentEvent> { fun handle(event: E) }

fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { ... }

Now an audit handler written for every event fits any subscription: bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured::class, audit) compiles with audit: Handler<PaymentEvent>. Delete the in and the same line fails with argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Handler<PaymentEvent>', but 'Handler<PaymentCaptured>' was expected. Java has no declaration-site variance, so the Java version writes ? super E at every use. kotlinc writes that wildcard for you: the Java signature of the Kotlin subscribe is subscribe(KClass<E>, Handler<? super E>), which is why Java callers in lesson 3 get the same freedom.

Why a fun interface and not the function type (E) -> Unit? A function type is already in on its parameter, so variance would be free. But Java would see a Function1<? super E, Unit>, and every Java lambda would have to end with return Unit.INSTANCE. A fun interface with a void method takes a plain Java lambda. Lesson 3 is about exactly that surface.

Inside the bus, handlers of different types share one map, so each one is stored behind an adapter that takes any PaymentEvent:

Java
Handler<PaymentEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event));
Kotlin
val adapter = Handler<PaymentEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) }

The generics workshop used safeCast, so a wrong event became a no-op. Here the dispatch keys already guarantee the type, so a mismatch can only be a bug in the bus, and cast makes that bug loud. The next section makes sure loud doesn't mean fatal.

Kotlin callers get a reified wrapper, as Type erasure and reified type parameters showed: inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>) = subscribe(E::class, handler). It needs no noinline. Only parameters of function type are inlined, and a Handler is an ordinary object.

In the demo, delete in and predict which two lines break.

sections.h: Observer rules: return a handle, isolate failures, iterate a snapshot
sections.html:
The bus is the subject from Observer and Command, so that lesson's three rules apply, and the lab tests each one.

subscribe returns a handle. Subscription extends AutoCloseable, and closing it removes exactly the adapter that subscribe stored. Without a handle, a handler owned by a short-lived object stays in the map forever: a lapsed listener that keeps reacting to events and can't be garbage collected.

One failing handler must not stop the others. deliver catches Exception around each call and reports it, with the event, to an ErrorHandler the bus was built with:

Java
for (Handler<PaymentEvent> handler : handlers) {     // a snapshot: copy-on-write
    called++;
    try {
        handler.handle(event);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        onError.onError(event, e);                    // one failure must not starve the rest
    }
}
Kotlin
for (handler in handlers) {                           // a snapshot: copy-on-write
    called++
    try {
        handler.handle(event)
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        onError.onError(event, e)                     // one failure must not starve the rest
    }
}

It catches Exception, not Throwable: an OutOfMemoryError should still take the service down. And the bus doesn't decide what an error means. Guava's EventBus catches and logs, and its own Javadoc says that "is rarely the right solution for error handling". Here the service passes in its own ErrorHandler, which can count the failure and send the event to a retry topic.

Each key's handlers live in a CopyOnWriteArrayList, so delivery iterates a snapshot. A handler may close its own subscription while it runs (a welcome email that fires once), and the loop carries on. With an ArrayList the next step of the loop throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copy-on-write makes subscribe copy the array, which is fine: subscriptions change at start-up, and events arrive all day.

Those two collections also make the bus safe for many publishers with no lock of its own. ConcurrentHashMap guards the registry, and each list is replaced, never changed in place. The lab's load test runs eight publishers while another thread subscribes and closes in a loop, and counts every event.

One rule doesn't change: delivery is synchronous. Every handler runs on the publisher's thread, which for a Kafka consumer is the poll loop. The design review in lesson 3 comes back to that.

The demo runs the same three handlers on three buses. Predict what each run prints before you run it.

code.title: IsolationDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.isolation import workbench.events.l02.demo.PaymentCaptured import workbench.events.l02.demo.PaymentEvent import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // The event model (PaymentEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. /** A list of handlers, stored in [handlers]; publish can isolate failures or not. */ class Bus(private val handlers: MutableList<(PaymentEvent) -> Unit>, private val isolate: Boolean) { fun subscribe(handler: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { handlers += handler return AutoCloseable { handlers -= handler } } fun publish(event: PaymentEvent) { for (h in handlers) { if (!isolate) { h(event); continue } try { h(event) } catch (e: Exception) { println(" (error handler: ${e.message})") } } } } fun scenario(title: String, bus: Bus) { println(title) var once: AutoCloseable? = null once = bus.subscribe { println(" welcome email, once"); once?.close() } // unsubscribes itself bus.subscribe { throw IllegalStateException("ledger is down") } bus.subscribe { println(" receipt for ${it.paymentId}") } try { bus.publish(PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)) bus.publish(PaymentCaptured("pay_7782", 250)) } catch (e: Exception) { println(" publish threw $e") } } fun main() { scenario("ArrayList, no isolation:", Bus(ArrayList(), isolate = false)) scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, no isolation:", Bus(CopyOnWriteArrayList(), isolate = false)) scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, isolated:", Bus(CopyOnWriteArrayList(), isolate = true)) }

import java.util.function.Consumer; public class IsolationDemoJava { sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured { String paymentId(); } record PaymentCaptured(String paymentId, long cents) implements PaymentEvent {} /** A list of handlers, stored in the list you pass; publish can isolate failures or not. */ static final class Bus { private final List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>> handlers; private final boolean isolate; Bus(List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>> handlers, boolean isolate) { this.handlers = handlers; try.expect: The ArrayList bus prints the welcome email and then publish threw java.util.ConcurrentModificationException, because the list changed under its own loop. The copy-on-write bus without isolation gets past that and dies on ledger is down; no receipt is sent. The isolated bus sends both receipts and reports two errors. With the narrower catch, the third run fails like the second: the IllegalStateException is no longer caught.

sections.h: Middleware is a chain, timing is a decorator
sections.html:
Some extra behavior belongs to every event once: logging, tracing, dropping a Kafka redelivery. Some belongs to one handler: timing the ledger, retrying the receipt email. The first kind is a chain of responsibility around publish. The second is a decorator around one handler. They look alike, and choosing the wrong one gives the wrong numbers.

The chain is the one from State and Chain of Responsibility. Each middleware gets the event and next, the rest of the chain, and either passes the event on or returns 0 to stop it. The bus builds the chain once, at construction, by folding a copy of the list from the right, so the first middleware wraps all the others and the last one wraps delivery:

Java
Next pipeline = this::deliver;
for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    Middleware m = middleware.get(i);
    Next rest = pipeline;
    pipeline = event -> m.intercept(event, rest);
}
Kotlin
private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList()
    .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } }

Order is behavior. With [dedupe, logging] a redelivery is dropped before anything logs it. With [logging, dedupe] it is logged and then dropped, which is what you want when you need to count redeliveries. Pick one and pin it in a test. The dedupe middleware itself is one line, if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0. add is the check and the act in one step, the fix from Race conditions: why count++ lies, so eight consumer threads can't all let the same capture through. Its "same event" is data-class equality: same type, same id, same amount.

The decorator is the one from Decorator and Proxy: it implements the same Handler<E>, adds one behavior and forwards the call.

Java
static <E extends PaymentEvent> Handler<E> timed(Handler<E> inner, String name, Timings timings) {
    return event -> {
        long start = timings.ticker().nanos();
        try { inner.handle(event); }
        finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker().nanos() - start); }
    };
}
Kotlin
fun <E : PaymentEvent> Handler<E>.timed(name: String, timings: Timings): Handler<E> {
    val inner = this
    return Handler { event ->
        val start = timings.ticker.nanos()
        try { inner.handle(event) } finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker.nanos() - start) }
    }
}

It records in finally, so a handler that throws is timed too, and the exception still reaches the bus's isolation. The clock is a Ticker you pass in. Tests use a fake one that moves forward by a fixed step on every read, so they check exact numbers with no sleeps and no flaky margins. A timing middleware couldn't do this job: it sees one delivery to all of an event's handlers, so it would add the ledger's 2 ms to the receipt email's 300 ms.

In the demo, swap the first two middleware and predict what the redelivery prints.

try.title: Reorder the chain
steps: Run ChainDemo and read the nesting of the > and < lines.
Swap logging("outer") and dropDuplicates() in the list. Predict what the redelivery prints now, and run.
Change tick() to add 90,000 instead of 40,000. Predict the ledger took line before you run.

code.title: ChainDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.chain import workbench.events.l02.demo.PaymentCaptured import workbench.events.l02.demo.PaymentEvent // The event model (PaymentEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. fun interface Next { fun proceed(event: PaymentEvent): Int } fun interface Middleware { fun intercept(event: PaymentEvent, next: Next): Int } fun interface Handler { fun handle(event: PaymentEvent) } /** Chain of responsibility: each middleware passes the event on, or answers 0 itself. */ fun chain(middleware: List<Middleware>, deliver: Next): Next = middleware.foldRight(deliver) { m, next -> Next { e -> m.intercept(e, next) } } fun logging(name: String) = Middleware { event, next -> println("$name > ${event.paymentId}") val called = next.proceed(event) println("$name < ${event.paymentId}: $called handler(s)") called } fun dropDuplicates(): Middleware { val seen = HashSet<PaymentEvent>() return Middleware { event, next -> if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0 } } /** Decorator: the same Handler interface, plus timing. Virtual time keeps the output stable. */ var clock = 0L fun tick(): Long { clock += 40_000; return clock } // every read moves the clock by 40 microseconds fun Handler.timed(name: String): Handler = Handler { event -> val start = tick() try { handle(event) } finally { println(" $name took ${(tick() - start) / 1_000} us") } } fun main() { val ledger = Handler { println(" ledger posts ${it.paymentId}") }.timed("ledger") val pipeline = chain( listOf(logging("outer"), dropDuplicates(), logging("inner")), // Step 2: swap the first two Next { e -> ledger.handle(e); 1 }, ) val capture = PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999) pipeline.proceed(capture) println("-- the same capture again (a Kafka redelivery)") pipeline.proceed(capture.copy()) }

alt.title: ChainDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l02.demo.chain; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; public class ChainDemoJava { sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured { String paymentId(); } record PaymentCaptured(String paymentId, long cents) implements PaymentEvent {} @FunctionalInterface interface Next { int proceed(PaymentEvent event); } @FunctionalInterface interface Middleware { int intercept(PaymentEvent event, Next next); } @FunctionalInterface interface Handler { void handle(PaymentEvent event); /** Decorator: the same Handler interface, plus timing. Virtual time keeps the output stable. */ default Handler timed(String name) { return event -> { long start = tick(); try { handle(event); } finally { System.out.println(" " + name + " took " + (tick() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } }; } } static long clock = 0; static long tick() { clock += 40_000; return clock; } // every read moves the clock by 40 microseconds /** Chain of responsibility: each middleware passes the event on, or answers 0 itself. */ static Next chain(List<Middleware> middleware, Next deliver) { Next next = deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = next; next = e -> m.intercept(e, rest); } return next; } static Middleware logging(String name) { return (event, next) -> { System.out.println(name + " > " + event.paymentId()); int called = next.proceed(event); System.out.println(name + " < " + event.paymentId() + ": " + called + " handler(s)"); return called; }; } static Middleware dropDuplicates() { Set<PaymentEvent> seen = new HashSet<>(); return (event, next) -> seen.add(event) ? next.proceed(event) : 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { Handler ledger = ((Handler) e -> System.out.println(" ledger posts " + e.paymentId())).timed("ledger"); Next pipeline = chain( List.of(logging("outer"), dropDuplicates(), logging("inner")), // Step 2: swap the first two e -> { ledger.handle(e); return 1; }); PaymentCaptured capture = new PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999); pipeline.proceed(capture); System.out.println("-- the same capture again (a Kafka redelivery)"); pipeline.proceed(new PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)); } }

try.expect: First run: outer >, inner >, the ledger lines, then inner < and outer < in reverse. The redelivery prints outer > and outer <: 0 handler(s): logged, then dropped. After the swap the redelivery prints nothing at all below the -- line. With 90,000 per read, ledger took 90 us: the decorator reads the clock twice, so the time is exactly one step.

analogy: Picture a newspaper's wire desk. A story about a football transfer goes to the football editor first, then to the sports editor, then to the chief editor, who wants everything: the most specific desk first, then each wider one. Before any editor sees it, a clerk stamps it and throws away a copy that already came in. One editor who spills coffee on his copy doesn't stop the others from reading theirs. The analogy breaks in one place: in a newsroom each editor gets a separate copy at the same moment. This bus hands the same object to each handler in turn, on one thread, so a slow editor makes everyone after him wait.
world: Quarkus has a bus like this built in: CDI events, fired with Event<T>.fire(...) and received by @Observes methods, and an observer of a supertype receives its subtypes too. Knowing the mechanism tells you what to check there: the delivery order, what happens when an observer throws, and which thread runs it. In a Kafka consumer the publisher's thread is the poll loop. If the handlers for one batch of records take longer than max.poll.interval.ms in total, the consumer is considered failed and the group rebalances. In a Temporal worker, publish from activities. Workflow code is replayed and must stay deterministic, so it shouldn't trigger in-process side effects at all.
mistake: The common mistake is doing slow work inside a handler: an HTTP call to the email provider, a database write with retries. The bus makes publish look like fire-and-forget, so it feels free. It isn't: delivery is synchronous, so a 300 ms receipt call makes every capture 300 ms slower, and the Kafka consumer that published it falls behind. The fix is to keep handlers fast and hand slow work to something built for it: write a row to an outbox table in the same transaction, or put the work on a bounded executor. Then time each handler with the decorator, so the next slow one shows up in a metric before it shows up in the lag.

compare.title: The bus in Java and Kotlin

java.title: EventBus.java
java.html: @FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E extends PaymentEvent> { void handle(E event); } @FunctionalInterface interface ErrorHandler { void onError(PaymentEvent event, Exception error); } @FunctionalInterface interface Next { int proceed(PaymentEvent event); } @FunctionalInterface interface Middleware { int intercept(PaymentEvent event, Next next); } final class EventBus { private final Map<Class<?>, List<Handler<PaymentEvent>>> registry = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final Map<Class<?>, List<Class<?>>> keyCache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final ErrorHandler onError; private final Next pipeline; EventBus(List<Middleware> middleware, ErrorHandler onError) { this.onError = onError; Next next = this::deliver; for (Middleware m : List.copyOf(middleware).reversed()) { // reversed(): JDK 21 Next rest = next; next = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } this.pipeline = next; } <E extends PaymentEvent> AutoCloseable subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { Handler<PaymentEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); List<Handler<PaymentEvent>> handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()); handlers.add(adapter); return () -> handlers.remove(adapter); } int publish(PaymentEvent event) { return pipeline.proceed(event); } private int deliver(PaymentEvent event) { int called = 0; for (Class<?> key : keyCache.computeIfAbsent(event.getClass(), EventBus::dispatchKeys)) { for (Handler<PaymentEvent> h : registry.getOrDefault(key, List.of())) { called++; try { h.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); } } } return called; } private static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { /* breadth-first walk, as above */ } }

kotlin.title: EventBus.kt
kotlin.html: fun interface Handler<in E : PaymentEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun interface Next { fun proceed(event: PaymentEvent): Int } fun interface Middleware { fun intercept(event: PaymentEvent, next: Next): Int } class EventBus( middleware: List<Middleware> = emptyList(), private val onError: ErrorHandler = ErrorHandler.PRINT, ) { private val registry = ConcurrentHashMap<KClass<*>, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler<PaymentEvent>>>() private val keyCache = ConcurrentHashMap<Class<*>, List<KClass<*>>>() private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val adapter = Handler<PaymentEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } val handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } handlers += adapter return Subscription { handlers.remove(adapter) } } inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribe(E::class, handler) fun publish(event: PaymentEvent): Int = pipeline.proceed(event) private fun deliver(event: PaymentEvent): Int { var called = 0 for (key in dispatchKeys(event.javaClass)) { for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) { called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) } } } return called } private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) { /* the walk */ } }

compare.note: The mechanism is identical: the same registry, the same walk, the same adapter, the same fold and the same catch. The differences are in who writes what. Java writes Handler<? super E> at the use site; Kotlin declares in once and kotlinc puts the wildcard into the Java signature. Kotlin gets default arguments on the constructor and a reified subscribe<E> for its own callers; Java callers get neither until lesson 3 adds @JvmOverloads and a Class<E> overload. And Kotlin's Next(::deliver) turns a function reference into a fun interface object, where Java writes this::deliver against its functional interface.

worked.title: Wire up receipts, and put each concern in its place

steps.say: Every capture should send a receipt email. That's one handler for one event type. Subscribe it under PaymentCaptured, the most specific key, so it never sees a refund.
steps.code: val receipts = Handler<PaymentCaptured> { email.sendReceipt(it.paymentId, it.amount) } val receiptsSubscription = bus.subscribe<PaymentCaptured>(receipts)

alt.html: // the Java bus from the comparison below Handler<PaymentCaptured> receipts = e -> email.sendReceipt(e.paymentId(), e.amount()); AutoCloseable receiptsSubscription = bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured.class, receipts);

steps.say: The email provider fails about one call in two hundred. Isolation already keeps the ledger and the audit log running when it does. What the service still has to decide is what a failure means. Here the error handler counts it and puts the event on a retry topic.
steps.code: val bus = EventBus( middleware = listOf(DropDuplicates()), onError = ErrorHandler { event, error -> metrics.increment("handler.failures") retryTopic.send(event, error.toString()) }, )

alt.html: ErrorHandler onError = (event, error) -> { metrics.increment("handler.failures"); retryTopic.send(event, error.toString()); }; EventBus bus = new EventBus(List.of(new DropDuplicates()), onError);

steps.say: After a consumer rebalance Kafka redelivers the last few records, and the customer must not get two receipts. Deduplication applies to every event once, before any handler, so it's middleware, first in the list. A decorator on the receipts handler would dedupe receipts only, and the ledger would still post twice.
steps.code: middleware = listOf(DropDuplicates(), logging) // dedupe first: redeliveries are never logged

alt.html: List<Middleware> middleware = List.of(new DropDuplicates(), logging); // dedupe first: redeliveries are never logged

steps.say: How long does a receipt take? That's a question about one handler, so it's a decorator: wrap the handler, not the bus. The timings now show about 300 ms per capture under receipts, all of it on the consumer thread. That number is the case for moving the email to an outbox, which lesson 3's design review makes.
steps.code: bus.subscribe<PaymentCaptured>(receipts.timed("receipts", timings))

alt.html: bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured.class, timed(receipts, "receipts", timings)); // the static timed(...) from the last section

lab.title: Build the bus: dispatch, variance, isolation, chain and decorator
steps: The package starts with lesson 1's solution (Values.kt, Model.kt, Parsing.kt, Summary.kt). Don't edit Callers.kt: the tests reach your inline subscribe through it. Run the tests: all sixteen fail.

TODO 2, subscribe: build the adapter with type.cast, add it to the list for type with computeIfAbsent, and return a Subscription that removes that adapter.
TODO 3, deliver: loop over dispatchKeys(event.javaClass) (given), call each key's handlers in order, count the calls, and send any Exception to onError.
TODO 4, pipeline: fold a copy of middleware from the right, starting from Next(::deliver). TODO 5: the reified subscribe in one line.

hints: registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } returns the list for that key, creating it the first time. Keep a reference to it for the Subscription.
Subscription { handlers.remove(adapter) } builds the handle. remove returns false the second time, so closing twice is harmless.
for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) skips keys nobody subscribed to.
The fold: middleware.toList().foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { e -> m.intercept(e, next) } }. foldRight visits the last middleware first, so it ends up innermost.
DropDuplicates: if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0. A contains check followed by add lets two threads through with the same event.
In timed, keep val inner = this before the Handler { ... } lambda, call inner.handle(event) inside try, and record in finally.
lab.done: All sixteen tests in BusTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Delivery and the chain from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write deliver(event) (dispatch keys, handlers in order, a count, one try per handler) and the one expression that builds the middleware chain. Then answer: in [logging, dedupe], does a redelivery get logged?

answer.html: private fun deliver(event: PaymentEvent): Int { var called = 0 for (key in dispatchKeys(event.javaClass)) { for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) { // copy-on-write snapshot called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) } } } return called } private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } // [logging, dedupe]: yes. logging runs first, then dedupe returns 0.

alt.html: private int deliver(PaymentEvent event) { int called = 0; for (Class<?> key : dispatchKeys(event.getClass())) { for (Handler<PaymentEvent> handler : registry.getOrDefault(key, List.of())) { called++; try { handler.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); } } } return called; } Next next = this::deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = next; next = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } this.pipeline = next; // [logging, dedupe]: yes. logging runs first, then dedupe returns 0.

recap: Keying handlers by the exact class misses subscriptions to MoneyMovement and PaymentEvent. Walk the event's supertypes, nearest first, cache the walk per class, and look up each key.
A handler only consumes events, so it is Handler<in E>. A Handler<PaymentEvent> then fits any subscription, and Java sees Handler<? super E> without writing it.
Store each handler behind an adapter that takes any event and casts with type.cast. The keys guarantee the type, so a failed cast is a loud bus bug.
Return a handle from subscribe, catch Exception per handler and report it to an injected ErrorHandler, and iterate a copy-on-write list so a handler can unsubscribe itself.
What applies to every event once (logging, dedupe) is middleware: a chain built once by a fold, where order is behavior. What applies to one handler (timing) is a decorator.
Test timing with a fake Ticker that steps on every read: exact numbers, no sleeps.

explain.prompt: Walk a colleague through one publish(PaymentCaptured) in your bus, from the first middleware to the count that comes back, and say why each step is there.
explain.answer: The call enters the middleware chain that the constructor built once by folding a copy of the list. Each middleware runs its code on the way in and calls next; dedupe stops a redelivery here by returning 0, using seen.add so the check and the insert are one step. At the end of the chain, deliver gets the dispatch keys for PaymentCaptured from a per-class cache: PaymentCaptured, MoneyMovement, PaymentEvent. For each key it iterates a copy-on-write snapshot of the adapters stored there, so a handler can unsubscribe itself. Each adapter casts the event with type.cast and calls the real handler. Every call is wrapped in a try, so one failing handler is reported to the error handler and the rest still run. The number of calls comes back out through the chain, where logging can record it. A handler for any event fits under any key because Handler is declared in.

deeper.html:
Three extensions come up as soon as this bus meets real traffic.

Asynchronous delivery. Give the bus an Executor and let deliver submit each handler call instead of making it. Two things change. Errors no longer come back to the publisher, so the ErrorHandler becomes the only place they surface. And ordering is gone: two captures for the same payment can run in either order on two pool threads. If order per payment matters, and in a ledger it does, route each payment id to one single-threaded lane, for example lanes[abs(id.hashCode() % lanes.size)], which is what a Kafka partition does for you between services. Bound the executor's queue, or a slow handler turns into an OutOfMemoryError.

Generic events. This bus keys by KClass, which is enough because no event has a type parameter. If you ever publish an Envelope<PaymentCaptured>, the class key collapses every envelope into one, the problem from KClass, Class and type tokens. Key by KType from typeOf<T>() then, and know that the supertype walk gets harder: KType has no cheap "all supertypes" answer without kotlin-reflect.

Guava's own verdict. Guava's EventBus Javadoc now opens with "We recommend against using EventBus", and its list of reasons reads like a review of any in-process bus: cross-references between producer and subscriber are hard to find, it gives little control of threading, it has no backpressure, and it doesn't propagate exceptions. Lesson 3's design review starts from that list. An in-process bus is still the right tool for decoupling modules inside one service, as long as handlers stay fast and the events that must survive a crash also go to an outbox.
